extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining design patent applications, including obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103(a)) rejections and compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 (drawings/specification) for design claims. Contains form paragraphs, examiner notes, and evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-analogous art for surface-only modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When modifying the surface of a primary reference so as to provide it with an attractive appearance, it is immaterial whether the secondary reference is analogous art, since the modification does not involve a change in configuration or structure and would not have destroyed the characteristics (appearance and function) of the primary reference. (In re Glavas.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this principle when the alleged modification is purely ornamental (surface appearance) and does not alter configuration/structure; treat secondary reference as usable even if non-analogous in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of objective evidence (secondary considerations) to rebut prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a prima facie case of obviousness has been established, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut it with objective evidence of nonobviousness. Examples of secondary considerations are commercial success, expert testimony and copying of the design by others. Any objective evidence or rebuttal evidence submitted by applicant, including affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, must be considered by examiners in determining patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must evaluate submitted secondary considerations and weigh them against the prima facie case; see MPEP § 716–716.06 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success requires nexus to the ornamental design
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence of commercial success is submitted, examiners must evaluate it to determine whether there is objective evidence of success, and whether the success can be attributed to the ornamental design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 have minimal evidentiary value on commercial success if there is no nexus between sales of the article and the ornamental features of the design (Avia Group Int’l Inc. v. L.A. Gear; In re Nalbandian). Examiners should require a clear nexus before giving weight to commercial-success evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission of expert testimony must establish the professional credentials of the person signing the affidavit or declaration, and should not express an opinion on the ultimate legal issue of obviousness since this conclusion is one of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure expert declarations set forth qualifications and factual observations; discount statements that directly assert obviousness or nonobviousness (Avia Group; Panduit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight to be given to copying by competitors
rubrics_metrics.description: With regard to evidence showing that competitors are copying the design, more than the mere fact of copying is necessary to make that action significant because copying may be attributable to other factors such as lack of concern for patent property or indifference with regard to the patentee’s ability to enforce the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and require evidence that copying is due to the claimed ornamental design (Cable Electric Products v. Genmark). Mere copies without context are insufficient to rebut obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away as a rebuttal to obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness can be rebutted if the applicant can show that the art in any material respect 'taught away' from the claimed invention. A reference teaches away when a person of ordinary skill, upon reading the reference, would be led in a direction divergent from the path taken by the applicant. (In re Haruna.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit discouragement or negative statements in references that would have deterred the designer of ordinary skill from the claimed design; treat such teaching away as significant rebuttal evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of design patentability: overall appearance, not minute details
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unobviousness in the overall appearance of the claimed design, when compared with the prior art, rather than minute details or small variations in design, that constitutes the test of design patentability. (See In re Frick; In re Lamb.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When providing a rationale for a 103(a) rejection, focus on whether the overall visual impression would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill, not on trivial or inconsequential differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining multiple references: relatedness and ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Modification of the primary reference in light of the secondary reference is proper because the applied references are so related that the appearance of features shown in one would suggest application of those features to the other. Case law holds that a designer skilled in the art is charged with knowledge of the related art; combination of old elements would have been within ordinary skill. (In re Rosen; In re Carter; In re Glavas; In re Antle; In re Nalbandian.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting a combination rejection, explain how the references are related and why one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine the ornamental features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections based on commonly assigned or copending applications (102(e)/103(a)) and how to overcome them
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conflicting design is commonly assigned or in a copending application/patent, it may qualify as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) and form the basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a). Such a rejection can be overcome by showing that the conflicting designs were commonly owned at the time the design in this application was made, or by establishing derivation or an earlier invention date under 37 CFR 1.131/1.132.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate form paragraphs (e.g., ¶15.19.02, ¶15.19.03) and advise applicants of the available responses: statements of common ownership, derivation proofs, dates of invention, mergers/continuations, or terminal disclaimers where applicable. Apply the AIPA rules for determining 102(e) dates where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional rejections where the reference discloses but does not claim the design
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) may be made where a copending application or earlier-filed document discloses the design in drawings but does not claim it; the provisional rejection is based on a presumption of future publication or patenting of the conflicting application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such provisional rejections may be overcome by showing derivation, an earlier date of invention, or common ownership at the relevant time; provide an explanation of differences and follow with form paragraphs (e.g., 15.70 and 15.67/15.68).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing disclosure is incorporated into the claim ('as shown' / 'as shown and described')
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing in a design application is incorporated into the claim by use of the claim language 'as shown.' The drawing disclosure can be supplemented by narrative description in the specification; such description is incorporated into the claim by 'as shown and described.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the combination of drawings and any descriptive text as defining the scope of the claimed design when assessing compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine scope under 35 U.S.C. 112 (second paragraph) before enablement (first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any analysis for compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 should begin with a determination of whether the claims satisfy the requirements of the second paragraph before moving on to the first paragraph. A determination of the scope of protection sought by the claim must be made because the drawing disclosure and any narrative description are incorporated into the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First identify the scope of the claimed design (what is being claimed) — then determine whether the disclosure enables a designer of ordinary skill to make an article having that shape and appearance. If the visual disclosure is inadequate to determine scope, the claim may fail both paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limited to surfaces shown in full lines and any written description; title does not define scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a claimed design is understood to be limited to those surfaces or portions of the article shown in the drawing in full lines in combination with any additional written description in the specification. The title does not define the scope of the claimed design but merely identifies the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the claim protects what is shown and described; if visible portions are not shown they are prima facie not part of the claim. Use MPEP §1503.01 guidance and case law (e.g., In re Zahn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Only visible surfaces at point of sale or during use need be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those surfaces of the article that are visible at the point of sale or during use must be disclosed to meet the requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs. Hidden surfaces not seen during sale or use are not required to be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings should illustrate the design as it will appear to purchasers and users. Examiners should accept omission of hidden surfaces unless they are part of the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive statements for flat, unornamented visible surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: While it is not necessary to show in the drawing those visible surfaces that are flat and devoid of surface ornamentation, they should be described in the specification by way of a descriptive statement if they are considered part of the claimed design. Such descriptive statements may not be used to describe visible surfaces which include structure that is clearly not flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptive statements cautiously: they are acceptable for flat, unornamented surfaces but not to define complex/three-dimensional visible structure that is not shown in the drawings (Philco Corp. v. Admiral Corp.; MPEP §1503.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: When drawings/specification omit visible parts, examiner should state omitted parts form no part of claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications in which the title defines an entire article but the drawings and specification fail to disclose portions or surfaces of the article that would be visible either during use or on sale will not be considered to violate 35 U.S.C. 112 if those omitted surfaces form no part of the claimed design. Examiners should include a statement in the first Office action indicating that the surfaces or portions not shown are understood to form no part of the claimed design (form paragraph 15.85).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert form paragraph 15.85 (Undisclosed visible surface(s)/portion(s) not forming part of the claimed design) to notify applicant that unshown visible areas are considered outside the claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: When rejecting under 35 U.S.C. 112 for drawing deficiencies, identify specific deficiencies and suggest cures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, as nonenabling and indefinite due to an insufficient drawing disclosure, examiners must specifically identify in the Office action what the deficiencies are in the drawing. A mere statement that the claim is nonenabling and indefinite due to poor quality of the drawing is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out the portions of the drawing that are insufficient to permit understanding of the shape and appearance, and, if possible, suggest how the rejection may be overcome (form paragraphs 15.21 and 15.20.02 may be used).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistencies between drawing views and resulting actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When inconsistencies between the views of the drawings are so great that the overall appearance of the design is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, as nonenabling and indefinite. Otherwise, inconsistencies between drawing views will be objected to and correction required by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inconsistencies render the design's overall appearance unclear, issue a 112 rejection specifying all inconsistencies; if not, object and require correction (see MPEP §1503.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative descriptions cannot rely on vague 'variations' or 'equivalents' absent drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: If a description in the specification refers to embodiments or modified forms not shown in the drawing, or includes vague and nondescriptive words such as 'variations' and 'equivalents,' or a statement indicating that the claimed design is not limited to the exact shape and appearance shown in the drawing, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, as nonenabling and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such descriptions fail to enable a designer to make the other embodiments without additional drawing views and fail to particularly point out/stringently claim those shapes; use form paragraph 15.21 to reject for these reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested responses to overcome 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections for drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is suggested that applicant may submit large, clear informal drawings or photographs which show the unclear areas in order that the examiner may determine if the claim may be clarified without adding new matter. Alternatively, applicant may disclaim the areas by converting them to broken lines and amend the specification to state that the broken-line portions form no part of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracketed text, identify unclear areas; provide applicants the option of supplying clearer drawings/photos or disclaiming via broken lines (form paragraph 15.20.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment may be impossible (fatal defects due to original disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim might be fatally defective; that is, it might not be possible to correct the claimed design without introducing new matter (35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure is so deficient that correction would introduce new matter, advise applicant the claim may be fatally defective (form paragraph 15.65). Consider rejecting under 112 where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to submit corrected drawing sheets to cure drawing deficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to submit replacement correction sheets overcoming all of the deficiencies in the drawing disclosure, or an explanation why the drawing corrections or additional drawing views are not necessary, will result in the rejection of the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs, being made FINAL in the next Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise applicants that corrected drawing sheets are required to avoid a final 112 rejection (form paragraph 15.73).
